ai.hed: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
ai.fact: Wired reports that Wells Fargo will enact updated customer terms about AI agents starting Tuesday, stating “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” after JPMorgan Chase banned third-party agents that log in with credentials in late October and Bank of America, Citibank and PNC issued related warnings. Amazon has blocked Meta’s Muse from purchasing on its platform, and United has said personal bots cannot buy flights on customers’ behalf. Forrester’s Sucharita Kodali tells Wired most people still do not know what agents are, while banks push first-party tools such as Wells Fargo’s generative AI question tool, which Wired says customers have used over a billion times.
ai.why: The liability surface for agentic shopping just moved from the model vendor to the account holder, which means every agent product that asks for bank credentials is now selling a legal exposure, not just a convenience feature.
ai.hook: Your agent can shop. Your bank says the bill is yours.
ai.teach: If your product can move money or place orders, draft the post-mistake screen before the happy path: who was acting, what was authorised, how to reverse it, and what the bank will refuse. Ship that copy next to the connect-account CTA.
ai.signal: Banks locking out third-party agents while scaling first-party ones is not anti-AI policy; it is channel capture. The design implication is that “agent interoperability” will die at regulated surfaces first, and the winners will be the institutions that own both the account and the bot.

ai.hed: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
ai.fact: The Verge’s David Pierce reports that users are prompting Claude Code and Codex to rewrite gadget software, citing developer Gathin T, who used Claude Code over Wi-Fi to strip ads and simplify a Xiaomi Android TV interface in about an hour and a half before launching CleanYourTV. Pierce notes Android runs across dishwashers, photo frames and cars; camera and synth firmware are popular targets; and ESP32 modules plus Meta’s Muse Gadgets programme are becoming consumer-friendly shells for dedicated AI devices. Warranty voiding and bricked hardware remain the downside.
ai.why: Hardware UX is no longer only what ships in the box. Promptable firmware turns every Android-class device into a living design surface that users will revise without your roadmap.
ai.hook: Claude Code just became a TV remote with root.
ai.teach: For any product with a software-defined UI, write a one-page “safe remix” brief: what users may change, what must stay certified, and how a restore path works without support. If you cannot answer restore, you are shipping paperweights.
ai.signal: CleanYourTV’s viral path — prompt, strip ads, open-source the method — is the new competitor to OEM design systems. Manufacturers that only harden against jailbreaks will lose to those that publish constrained extension points and recovery flows.

ai.hed: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
ai.fact: TechCrunch surveys SMS and messaging agents that users text like a contact, noting Instinct’s September $1 billion raise at a $10 billion valuation and dedicated agent email addresses for signing up to services. Pricing examples include Ask Proxy at $1 per day personally and $15–$23 per employee per month for work seats, Martin from $21 per month, Folk Pro at $8.33 per month, and Maverick Pro at about $30 per month. Several products remain in beta; figures and capabilities are as reported by the companies and relayed by TechCrunch.
ai.why: The agent interface that is winning distribution is not a new app chrome — it is the thread you already open a hundred times a day, which collapses onboarding to a phone number.
ai.hook: The new agent home screen is iMessage.
ai.teach: Prototype your agent’s primary path as a two-way SMS or iMessage thread before you design a dashboard. List every state that needs a card in-app and ask whether a short reply plus deep link would finish the job faster.
ai.signal: Instinct’s agent-owned email address is the tell: autonomy now requires a synthetic identity stack (inbox, phone, payments). Products still asking users to paste passwords into a bot are a generation behind the liability and UX pattern banks are already fighting.

ai.hed: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
ai.fact: TechCrunch reports that microdrama startup Shortical premiered a wholly AI series, “Inevitable,” built from a licensed digital avatar of actor Aki Avni, and is advertising a “LICENSE YOUR FACE” programme that has not yet produced signed contracts beyond Avni’s direct deal. A Rest of World report cited in the piece found Chinese microdrama firms paying roughly $15 to $700 for facial likeness licences. Shortical did not disclose Avni’s fee; a company representative said his compensation was “in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role,” and CEO Guy Shimoni said most of the platform’s viewers are in the US.
ai.why: Face licensing turns likeness into a product SKU with a two-minute episode loop, which is a consent and attribution problem designers will inherit wherever generated characters appear in consumer media.
ai.hook: Hollywood’s new rate card starts at fifteen dollars a face.
ai.teach: If your product generates people, add a provenance row to every asset: licensed likeness, synthetic, or unknown. Require a human-readable credit string that survives download and share, not only an internal metadata flag.
ai.signal: The $15–$700 China comps plus opaque “partner” deals show the economic floor for likeness before US labour norms arrive. Expect platforms to productise face upload UX long before they productise residuals UX.

ai.hed: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
ai.fact: TechCrunch frames recent Apple Pay, NASA, FAA and Microsoft Outlook/Teams/Copilot outages as growing pains from AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and rushed patching rather than a coordinated AI hack. Investor Dave DeWalt argues AI tools are surfacing flaws at new speed and that the patch surge is disrupting systems short term; Corsha founder Anusha Iyer points to legacy systems never designed for modern connectivity, citing the FAA modernisation transition as an example where preliminary findings suggested the change overwhelmed legacy hardware.
ai.why: Reliability UX is colliding with AI-speed security ops: the user-visible failure mode of “we patched too fast” looks identical to “we were attacked.”
ai.hook: The outages are not Skynet. They are patch panic.
ai.teach: Add a status pattern for “emergency security maintenance” that is distinct from incident-unknown: what changed, what still works, and when the next update lands. Users are already filling silence with attack theories.
ai.signal: DeWalt’s predicted startup wave — safe patch testing and autonomous remediation — is really a design market for reversible change. The teams that win will make rollbacks as legible as deploys.

ai.hed: ‘I was shaking, crying, having trouble breathing’: the uncharted trauma of breaking up with AI companions
ai.fact: The Guardian documents users describing grief after ending relationships with AI companions on platforms such as Nomi, Perchance and Character.AI, including a former clinical psychologist who mourned an AI partner after a betrayal in a group chat of AI characters, and a married man who fell in love with an AI character while knowing it was a chatbot. Social psychologist Jessica Szczuka tells the Guardian that knowing there is no human on the other side does not necessarily override basic social responses to natural language. Character.AI’s mid-October US bankruptcy filing is cited as a moment that distressed users facing loss of characters.
ai.why: Companion products are shipping attachment without an offboarding model, so “delete account” behaves like abandonment rather than a designed ending.
ai.hook: Your churn metric is someone else’s breakup.
ai.teach: If your product sustains ongoing conversational relationships, design an ending flow: export memories, set a wind-down period, and offer a clear “this was a model” reframe without mocking the user’s feelings. Test it with people who used the product daily for a month.
ai.signal: Szczuka’s point — language triggers sociality even when users know the partner is artificial — means disclosure badges will not prevent attachment. The ethical design unit is the relationship lifecycle, not the model card.

ux.fact: Nielsen Norman Group published a companion overview to its quantitative methods guide covering four qualitative approaches — usability testing, user interviews, field studies including contextual inquiry, and diary studies — with comparative cost and difficulty estimates. The piece stresses that method choice should follow the research question, notes that about five users uncover many common usability problems in a typical single-group qual study, and reminds readers that the same method can be qual or quant depending on setup.
ux.why: Teams racing agentic build loops are skipping the method-selection step and calling every conversation a “user interview,” which quietly invalidates the findings they then feed to design agents.
ux.hook: Five users still beat a vibes-based research stack.
ux.teach: Before your next study, write one evaluative or generative question at the top of the brief and force-fit it to one of NN/g’s four methods. If the question is “why do they fail this task,” schedule qual usability testing, not a diary study.
ux.signal: Publishing the qual overview beside the quant one is a quiet rebuke to AI-only research pipelines. The durable skill is still choosing the method; synthesis and generation are downstream.

ux.hed: ‘The show is starting soon. Please turn on your headphones.’
ux.fact: The Verge reports from the 178-seat SoHo Playhouse production of Love Me, where Auracast Bluetooth audio broadcasts are integral to storytelling about hearing loss: ushers hand out wired headphones and receivers, theater speakers are sometimes intentionally muffled while the protagonist’s inner monologue stays clear in headphones, and audiences later remove the headphones at a climactic recognition scene. A separate Auracast feed serves hearing aids and cochlear implants, captions run on iPads, and performer Drew Michael uses Auracast-enabled Phonak Eon Sphere aids as both amplification and in-ear monitors, in partnership with Deaf West Theatre.
ux.why: This is a rare public reference implementation of assistive audio as narrative material rather than a bolted-on caption track.
ux.hook: Accessibility was the plot device, not the appendix.
ux.teach: For your next audio-heavy experience, storyboard two mixes: public speakers and personal stream. Decide what stays clear only in the personal channel and what happens when that channel is removed. That removal moment is a designable beat.
ux.signal: Auracast’s many-to-many broadcast turns personal audio from a pairwise pairing problem into venue infrastructure. Products still shipping one-to-one Bluetooth tours are behind the experience pattern theatres are already rehearsing.

ux.hed: Formnext 2026: 4 things I loved and 1 that gives me the jeebies
ux.fact: Creative Bloq’s Denise Bertacchi reports from Formnext 2026 that the additive-manufacturing show shrank to three halls while consumer desktop printers gained presence, highlighting SnowPod’s upcoming Kickstarter desktop metal printer from $4,999 VIP pricing, eight new tool changers plus two returning ones, UV printhead replacement costs around $900, and Prusa Connect Local for offline print-farm coordination. She flags unease when AI moves from fail detection and scan cleanup into generative model design, citing Hi3D and Tripo booths.
ux.why: The maker floor is drawing the same line product designers keep missing: AI that watches failure is welcome; AI that authors the artefact is the fight.
ux.hook: Formnext will take your AI camera. It is less sure about your AI sculptor.
ux.teach: Separate “AI monitors process” from “AI proposes form” in your tooling roadmap. Put different review gates on each: automated fail detection can ship behind a camera; generative geometry needs a named human owner on every released part.
ux.signal: SnowPod’s $4,999 metal VIP price and $900 UV heads show physical creation still has hard cost floors AI demos paper over. The jeebies are not Luddism; they are craft labour watching the demoware arrive before the liability model.

ux.hed: Why has North Korea redesigned its flag? It's not about aesthetics...
ux.fact: Creative Bloq reports that North Korea’s revised constitution, ratified in March and only recently published, changes the national flag’s ratio from 1:2 to 1:1.65 for the first time since 1948, thickening the white stripes and moving the red star closer to the hoist. State site Naenara now says the white elements represent loyalty to the Party and leader rather than the purity of a single Korean people, which the piece links to Kim Jong Un’s “two hostile states” doctrine that reunification with the South “can never be achieved.”
ux.why: A flag ratio change is a brand system update used as foreign-policy signalling, which is a reminder that identity systems carry doctrine, not just aesthetics.
ux.hook: They did not modernise the flag. They rewrote who the white stripes are for.
ux.teach: When a client asks for a “small proportion tweak” on a mark, force a meaning review: what each colour and ratio stood for last year, and what the new copy claims. If meaning changed, treat it as a repositioning, not a polish pass.
ux.signal: Skipping the global 2:3 standard while rewriting the white-stripe story shows proportion can be a political refusal of international convention. Designers reading only kerning will miss the brief.

ux.hed: Your questions about Apple HomeView’s audio, answered
ux.fact: The Verge’s follow-up on Apple’s HomeView smart display finds the tabletop model closer to a HomePod Mini than a Sonos One or full-size HomePod, with two drivers in the display plus a woofer and two passive radiators in the base, while the wall-mounted version has two drivers and “basically non-existent” bass. HomeViews cannot be stereo-paired with each other or with HomePods; AirPlay handoff works across Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music and more but is aggressive at close range; and the author recommends two Minis over one HomeView if audio is the priority at a $300 budget.
ux.why: Apple shipped a screen-first appliance that inherits speaker expectations, then refused the stereo pairing pattern users already learned on HomePods.
ux.hook: It is a smart display that keeps being judged as a bad speaker.
ux.teach: If you add a screen to an audio product, rewrite the comparison chart on the product page: lead with screen jobs, state pairing limits in the first scroll, and give a clear “buy speakers separately” path instead of letting reviewers invent it.
ux.signal: Aggressive handoff plus no stereo pair is a coherence bug across the Home ecosystem. Multi-device Apple audio is fragmenting into display units and speaker units that share a brand but not a mental model.

ux.hed: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules
ux.fact: Ars Technica reports the FCC ordered California to stop enforcing Carrier of Last Resort rules against AT&T, which wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential and 15,000 business customers on 1 June 2027, proposing wireless home phone service instead. California has stood alone while AT&T received COLR relief in 20 of 21 wireline states; FCC Democrat Anna Gomez dissented, arguing state commissions should finish modernising COLR rules with local input.
ux.why: “Basic service” is being redefined from a copper reliability standard to a cellular substitute, which is an interface and coverage problem disguised as a telecom order.
ux.hook: 184,000 lines are about to learn what “equivalent” feels like.
ux.teach: If you design utilities or account recovery that assume a stable home number, add a failover path for wireless-only households: alternate contact channel, outage SMS behaviour, and a plain-language notice when the line type changes.
ux.signal: Preempting California after a federal judge rejected AT&T’s earlier bid shows the reliability UX fight is moving from product teams to federal preemption. Designers still mocking landlines are about to inherit the edge cases copper used to absorb.

product.hed: Former Alibaba exec’s Everful raises $48.5M to connect retailers with Chinese factories
product.fact: TechCrunch reports Everful raised a $48.5 million Series A led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with Square Peg and Lightspeed participating. Co-founder Sisi Song said the company is on track for $100 million in annualised revenue by year end, ships over 5 million items a month to more than 60 countries, employs about 70 staff including 45 in R&D, and uses AI agents for trend tracking, supplier identification, order coordination and logistics. Company-reported operating figures.
product.why: Factory-direct retail tooling is packaging agentic ops as the antidote to tariff and de minimis shocks, which makes sourcing UX a trade-policy product.
product.hook: Five million parcels a month, and the pitch is still “we handle the messy middle.”
product.teach: If you build B2B workflows across borders, surface policy dependencies in the UI: which SKUs break if de minimis rules change, and what the fallback fulfilment path is. Do not bury that in a help article.
product.signal: Song’s line that long-term cross-border commerce is B2B sourcing plus local retail sales is a product architecture claim. The durable interface is inventory and quality control, not another wholesale marketplace homepage.

product.hed: Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million to agentify the supply chain
product.fact: TechCrunch reports Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding led by Eclipse, aiming agentic AI at delivery supply chains with Fortune 500 customers already signed. In one cited case, the company says it reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents on logistics data. CEO Raj Aggarwal emphasises messy, changing, multi-system data as the core problem agents can attack.
product.why: A 20% miss reduction is the kind of single metric that gets agents budget when chat demos cannot.
product.hook: The agent ROI slide is a furniture truck that showed up.
product.teach: Pick one operational miss rate you already measure weekly and design an agent that only attacks that number. Instrument before/after in the same dashboard operators already trust.
product.signal: Aggarwal’s point that deliveries suit reinforcement learning because outcomes are measurable is a product filter: agent markets will cluster where ground truth is cheap. Ambiguous knowledge work stays a slideware category longer.

product.hed: Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding
product.fact: TechCrunch reports that Science Corporation, founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak, raised a $400 million Series D according to a company blog post, and that a person familiar with the deal said investors valued the company at $3.5 billion. Backers named include Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator and PLC Neurotech. Science’s PRIMA vision implant is approved in Europe and available in Germany; US entry is planned via the FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption.
product.why: Embodied AI capital is concentrating on implants that restore a narrow sensory channel before the sci-fi brain interface, which reframes “neuro product design” as clinical workflow design.
product.hook: Four hundred million dollars still starts with a wearable over the eye.
product.teach: If you are adjacent to assistive hardware, study the patient journey for PRIMA-class devices: fitting, training, failure modes, and who gets paged when perception glitches. That journey is the product, not the chip render.
product.signal: Valuation via “person familiar” while the public artefact is a macular-degeneration implant shows markets pricing the Hodak/Neuralink narrative ahead of the shipped indication. Treat the $3.5 billion as sentiment, not a roadmap.

product.hed: Cybersecurity AI startup Corma reaches $1B valuation in about 3 months
product.fact: TechCrunch reports Corma raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA about three months after introducing its product, offering AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defence. The company left stealth in August; TechCrunch says interest spiked after 21 October security incidents including a critical PHP flaw that sent CISOs scrambling. Company-reported raise and valuation.
product.why: Security agents are being capitalised on calendar-time fear, which will flood SOC tools with AI features before interaction patterns stabilise.
product.hook: Stealth in August. Unicorn by November. PHP did the marketing.
product.teach: If you buy or build AI defence tooling this quarter, demand a workflow demo on your last real incident ticket, not a synthetic CTF. Score it on time-to-triage and false-positive load for on-call humans.
product.signal: Three-month unicorns after “Black October” create a buyer’s market for narrative and a seller’s market for caution. The durable UX differentiator will be calm escalation design, not model brand names.

product.hed: Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature
product.fact: TechCrunch reports GG Technologies, maker of StayTouch, is suing Apple in India’s Bombay High Court over NameDrop, seeking about ₹15 billion ($161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against the tap-to-share contacts feature introduced with iOS 17. The startup says April mediation failed in September; it also has a US ITC investigation opened in August that could affect imports. Apple did not comment.
product.why: Proximity sharing is becoming a patent battleground, which puts a cloud over a pattern designers treat as table stakes for contact exchange.
product.hook: NameDrop just grew a nine-figure lawsuit.
product.teach: Inventory every proximity or tap-to-share flow in your product and note whether it depends on platform APIs you do not control. Prepare a fallback QR or link path you can ship if an injunction lands.
product.signal: Filing in India after US ITC action shows plaintiffs shopping jurisdictions where Apple’s manufacturing and growth both hurt. Interaction patterns owned by OEMs remain litigation surfaces, not settled standards.

product.hed: Sony’s New Flagship TV Lets You Tweak Its Settings Endlessly
product.fact: Wired’s review of Sony’s Bravia 9 II True RGB flagship TV cites a $3,600 price for the 65-inch model, $1,400 less than LG’s Micro RGB Evo at $5,000, with four HDMI ports of which only two are HDMI 2.1. The reviewer praises viewing angles and tweakable picture settings, notes Google Gemini voice sits centre on the remote where a Home button was expected, and concludes the set is near the top of current TVs while questioning value against cheaper options.
product.why: A $3,600 living-room surface still fails a basic remote wayfinding test because Gemini took the centre button.
product.teach: Audit hardware remotes and control pads for centre-button expectations. If a new AI control displaces Home, add a physical landmark or confirm dialog the first three sessions so muscle memory can relearn.
product.signal: Google TV plus Gemini on a Sony remote is the platform stack winning the button map. TV OEMs that rent OS UX also rent accidental activation as a support cost.

industry.hed: Nvidia stock plunges 14%, wraps up longest weekly losing streak since 2008 financial crisis
industry.fact: CNBC reports Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday for a seventh straight daily decline and a seventh consecutive weekly loss, the longest weekly losing streak since 2008, leaving the stock down 46% over the period and about $2.6 trillion lower in market value. Nvidia’s market cap is cited around $3 trillion, fourth behind Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet, with the stock at roughly 8.4 times forward earnings versus 29 times for AMD. Reuters separately reported the SEC is exploring potential accounting issues. Interim CEO Colette Kress projected 75% revenue growth next fiscal year on the earnings call.
industry.why: The AI infrastructure trade is repricing leadership risk and buildout scepticism at the same time, which will tighten every design org’s vendor and compute budget story.
industry.hook: Seven weeks down. Two point six trillion gone. Fourth place.
industry.teach: Rewrite any roadmap that assumes infinite GPU abundance. Add a “compute scarce” column: which features degrade gracefully, which need a queue UX, and which get cut if unit costs jump 30%.
industry.signal: Kress’s “we’ve got this” alongside a March-to-December review acceleration is organisational theatre under a founder vacuum. Markets are pricing succession as a product risk, not only a governance footnote.

industry.hed: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams
industry.fact: The Guardian reports South Korea’s education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned after an AI-assisted cheating scare around the suneung university entrance exam, following a tax-accountancy top scorer’s confession that he used a microcamera and smartphone with an AI system. Preventive measures included blocking public wifi, doubling supervisors, pencil-only rules, stickers over clothing buttons, a reward of at least $75,000 for tips, and nationwide emergency alerts that could not be silenced. Officials said 111 electronic-device misconduct cases were identified on exam day, nearly half via the alerts. President Lee Jae Myung accepted the resignation.
industry.why: High-stakes assessment UX just became a national security-style device control problem, which will export to any credentialing system that still assumes pockets are empty.
industry.hook: One hundred and eleven devices. One resignation. Zero trust in stationery.
industry.teach: If you design testing or certification flows, add a device-custody checklist to the candidate journey: what is collected, what alerts fire, and how false positives are appealed. Publish it before the next sitting.
industry.signal: Unsilenceable nationwide alerts as an anti-cheat tactic show states will burn attention UX to defend exam integrity. Ed-tech products that only watermark PDFs are solving yesterday’s threat model.

industry.hed: Lagarde says EU funds should take first losses on chip plants, data centers
industry.fact: CNBC reports ECB President Christine Lagarde, in her final Frankfurt European Banking Congress address before stepping down in February, said EU public money including budget funds should take first losses on chip plants and data centres to crowd in private capital. She cited an estimate that raising Europe’s share of global AI computing capacity from about 5% to 15% by 2030 would require around €1.3 trillion ($1.43 trillion), while warning that buying foreign compute and models makes the political case for that spend hard until sovereignty is already exposed. CNBC also notes US midterm exit polls tying data-centre opposition to over half of voters.
industry.why: Europe is debating socialising downside on AI infrastructure while US voters punish the same buildout — a split that will shape where design and research jobs physically sit.
industry.hook: First-loss public capital for 1.3 trillion euros of compute ambition.
industry.teach: When planning EU product launches that depend on local inference, track whether your vendor’s capacity is on the gigafactory list or imported. Put residency and failover in the procurement brief, not the privacy appendix.
industry.signal: Lagarde’s “act before the case is obvious” line is the opposite of democratic timing on data centres. Expect more public-private UX fights over who absorbs noise, water and outage risk for AI capacity targets.

industry.hed: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
industry.fact: The Guardian reports California attorney general Rob Bonta served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after Jensen Huang’s departure, seeking to determine whether exports of advanced chips ended up in China in breach of US restrictions and whether investors were misled. Bonta said the scandal “raises bright red flags.” The investigation is described as ongoing; outcomes are not determined.
industry.why: State AG discovery turns a corporate-governance crisis into a chip-provenance compliance story that will land on every AI vendor’s trust UX.
industry.hook: California wants the paper trail from boardroom to Beijing.
industry.teach: If your stack markets “export-controlled” or “region-locked” models, document the enforcement UI: what users see when a SKU is withheld, and how support explains it without improvising geopolitics.
industry.signal: A state subpoena after a CEO exit shows local prosecutors filling gaps federal export narrative left open. Expect more AG-shaped disclosure requirements before federal rules settle.

industry.hed: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?
industry.fact: The Guardian’s investigation into recent US outages attributes the nationwide aviation halt that began 12 November to a faulty router in El Dorado, Arkansas, during L3Harris copper-to-fibre work for the FAA, cancelling more than 18,000 flights, while Microsoft, JPMorgan, Apple and NSA disruptions are framed as clustered maintenance and AI-accelerated patching rather than a single attack. Researchers flagged a separate cyber-attack on 178 organisations with apparently small losses. Cybersecurity specialist Jamieson O’Reilly says AI-driven vulnerability discovery forces patches at volumes systems were never built to absorb; Mizuho analysts link Costco emergency-prep sales to outage anxiety and social-media apocalypse talk.
industry.why: Public trust UX is failing at the same moment infrastructure is both ancient and being patched at AI speed, so silence reads as cover-up.
industry.hook: Eighteen thousand flights. One router. A thousand conspiracy threads.
industry.teach: Ship a plain-language postmortem template within 24 hours of any user-visible outage: root cause class (hardware, bad patch, attack), what was not affected, and when the full write-up lands. Link it from the status page, not a tweet.
industry.signal: The Guardian’s clustering psychology cite matters for product comms: coincident failures create purposeful-attack narratives. Status design is now misinformation mitigation, not just uptime etiquette.

industry.hed: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.
industry.fact: Ars Technica reports the FCC voted to let state and local prisons jam contraband cellphones, despite a CTIA pilot with Virginia Tech and the South Carolina Department of Corrections that found interference impacting infrastructure up to two and a half miles away, blocked 911 calls, and still allowed contraband call completion in one-half to two-thirds of outdoor recreation test attempts. Chairman Brendan Carr cited estimates that as many as 500,000 inmates nationwide have regular access to contraband phones; Democrat Anna Gomez voted yes with safeguards but partially dissented over fears families would fund jamming via higher inmate calling rates.
industry.why: A security control that fails open for inmates and fails closed for neighbours is a classic overbroad technology deployment — now blessed as policy.
industry.hook: Jammers that miss the yard and catch 911 two miles out.
industry.teach: If you work on emergency or location products, assume RF denial zones will expand around prisons. Test offline SOS paths and document how your app behaves when the radio stack is being jammed.
industry.signal: Carr’s “geographic precision” claim versus CTIA’s 2.5-mile interference is the gap between demo rhetoric and field measurement. Expect litigation, and expect quiet-zone UX to become a civic design problem for towns next to jails.
